title: Association between obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and COVID‐19 severity

sections.abstract:
Obstructive sleep apnea and sleep‐related hypoxia have been associated with higher rates of hospitalization and mortality among patients with Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19). We further explored the association between obstructive sleep apnea, COVID‐19 severity and related mortality. In addition, we examined the effects of clinical and demographic parameters on COVID‐19. In this retrospective study, we included adult patients who were diagnosed with COVID‐19 prior to the Omicron variant identification. We compared the severity of COVID‐19 and mortality with the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea. The study population included 44,275 patients who tested positive for COVID‐19. Of these, 97% had mild or asymptomatic disease, 1.2% had moderate disease, and 1.8% had severe disease. Obstructive sleep apnea was diagnosed in 980 (2.2%) patients. In a multivariate analysis, obstructive sleep apnea diagnosis increased the risk of severe COVID‐19 by 1.6 (95% confidence interval: 1.1–2.4) compared with mild disease. However, no increase in mortality was associated with obstructive sleep apnea. Interestingly, patients with moderate and high socioeconomic status had a 1.6 times higher risk for severe COVID‐19 than patients from the low socioeconomic status group (95% confidence interval: 1.2–2.1 and 95% confidence interval: 1.1–2.3, respectively). The risk of dying due to COVID‐19 was 1.6 (95% confidence interval: 1.1–2.5) and 3.1 (95% confidence interval: 1.8–5.3) times higher in patients with medium and high socioeconomic status, respectively, compared with patients with low socioeconomic status. Diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea was found to be an independent risk factor for severe COVID‐19. The higher the socioeconomic status, the higher the risk of severe COVID‐19 morbidity and mortality.

Keywords: continuous positive airway pressure, COVID‐19, obstructive sleep apnea, vaccine
sections.introduction:
At the beginning of the Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) pandemic, the lungs were the main target organ of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2; Synowiec et al., 2021 ). The clinical spectrum of COVID‐19 ranges from asymptomatic to severe, requiring hospitalization and mechanical ventilation, and may even lead to death. Comorbidities, particularly respiratory diseases, increase the risk of severe morbidity due to COVID‐19 (Aveyard et al., 2021 ; Miller & Cappuccio, 2021 ).

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common sleep disorder characterized by repeated upper airway blockages (partial or complete) during sleep, which can lead to hypoxic events. The major risk factors are obesity, male gender and older age. An effective treatment for OSA is use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) to eliminate the episodes of apneas and hypopneas and hypoxic events (Abbasi et al., 2021 ; Wellman et al., 2022 ).

Several recent studies have reported an association between OSA and the severity of COVID‐19. There are some reasons to believe that the severity of COVID‐19 increases in the presence of OSA. First, OSA is associated with old age, obesity, cardiovascular disease, hypertension and other factors, many of which are known to be risk factors for severe COVID‐19 (Malhotra & White, 2002 ; Yang et al., 2020 ). Secondly, the combination of hypoxia from OSA with hypoxia in COVID‐19 pneumonia could increase the likelihood of a poor prognosis of COVID‐19 infection (McSharry & Malhotra, 2020 ). In COVID‐19, hypoxia potentiates inflammation and coagulation due to endothelial injury, may trigger proinflammatory cytokines and exacerbate a cytokine storm, and promote viral replication, which could lead to poor outcomes (Pena Orbea et al., 2021 ). Other studies have suggested that OSA may also facilitate SARS‐CoV‐2 entry into host cells by causing dysregulation of the renin‐angiotensin system pathway that is involved in this process (Ekiz et al., 2020 ; Hariyanto & Kurniawan, 2021 ).

Clinical studies have demonstrated that sleep‐related hypoxia is associated with higher rates of hospitalization and mortality among patients with COVID‐19. Maas et al. demonstrated a 1.65 times (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.36–2.02) increased risk for hospitalization and 1.98 times (95% CI: 1.65–2.37) higher risk for respiratory failure due to COVID‐19 among patients with OSA (Maas et al., 2020 ). In another study, sleep‐related hypoxia was associated with a 31% higher rate of hospitalization and mortality (Pena Orbea et al., 2021 ).

This study aimed to explore the association between OSA diagnosis and COVID‐19 severity. Our hypothesis was that patients diagnosed with OSA are at an increased risk for severe COVID‐19.
sections.methods:
This retrospective study was conducted in the Dan Petah‐Tiqwa district of “Clalit Health Services” (CHS), the largest publicly funded Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) in Israel. The study population consisted of all patients, aged ≥ 18 years, men and women, who were diagnosed with COVID‐19 between March 2020 and 31 November 2021, before the advent of the new Omicron variant. Hospitalized patients were classified according to Israeli Health Ministry guidelines: mild disease (COVID‐19 symptoms), moderate disease (COVID‐19 pneumonia), and severe COVID‐19 (respiratory rate >30 and/or oxygen saturation ≤ 93% at room air and/or PaO 2 /FiO 2 < 300; Ministry of Health‐Gov, 2024 ). Patients who were not hospitalized were classified as asymptomatic or mild COVID‐19. For the entire study population, we researched for OSA diagnosis and CPAP purchases, and divided the population into two groups: patients with and without OSA. Patients with OSA were subdivided into those with and without CPAP purchases.

Data regarding the number of COVID‐19 vaccinations and Pfizer–BioNTech COVID‐19 vaccine (BNT162b2 mRNA) prior to COVID‐19 diagnosis were collected. Patients were also classified as those with at least one vaccination, at least 3 weeks (Abu‐Raddad et al., 2021 ; Hunter & Brainard, 2021 ) before their COVID‐19 diagnosis, or not vaccinated. We recorded data on age, gender, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits (never, past or current smoking), socioeconomic status (SES) and Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), which is a weighted score of age and chronic conditions (myocardial infarct, congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic pulmonary disease, connective tissue disease, ulcer disease, mild liver disease, diabetes, hemiplegia, moderate or severe renal diseases, diabetes with end organ damage, any tumour, leukaemia, lymphoma, moderate or severe liver disease, metastatic solid tumour and AIDS). We also recorded mortality due to COVID‐19. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Meir Medical Center, Kfar‐Saba, Israel (approval no. 0045‐22‐COM1).

Comparisons between the groups were made using t ‐tests or ANOVA for continuous variables, and chi‐squared or Fisher's exact tests (where the numbers were small) for categorical variables. We looked at correlations using Spearman's rank test for non‐parametric variables. Odds ratios were calculated using logistic regression for the two primary outcomes of COVID‐19; severity and mortality due to COVID‐19. Logistic regression was used in multivariate analyses that included age, gender, smoking history (past or current versus never), SES, CCI and COVID‐19 vaccination. Patients with missing data were excluded from the analyses. The statistical analysis was conducted using the R Project for Statistical Computing version 4.0.4 ( https://www.r-project.org/ ).
sections.results:
The study population included 44,275 patients who tested positive for SARS‐CoV‐2. Among them, 97% had mild or asymptomatic disease, 1.2% had moderate disease and 1.8% had severe disease (including death). The mean age of the study population was 43 (± 17) years, and 47% were men (Table 1 ). More patients were from the medium SES group (48%); however, of the rest, more patients were from low SES groups (29%) than the higher groups (20%). Data on smoking habits were missing for 22.7% of the study population. Most patients were never smokers (56.6%), whereas 20.7% had a history of current or past smoking. The mean CCI was 1.1 (± 2). Seventy percent of the study population had at least one COVID‐19 vaccine at least 3 weeks before their COVID‐19 diagnosis, with a mean number of 1.3 (± 1.1) vaccination. We did not find BMI data close to the COVID‐19 diagnosis in most of the study population.

Characteristics of the study population.

Abbreviations: CCI, Charlson Comorbidity Index; COVID‐19, Coronavirus disease 2019; CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; N/A, not available; OSA, obstructive sleep apnea; SD, standard deviation; SES, socioeconomic status.

Without N/A.

At least 3 weeks before COVID‐19 diagnosis.

Obstructive sleep apnea was diagnosed in 980 (2.2%) patients in the study population. Patients with OSA were significantly older than those without OSA (60 years versus 43 years, respectively, p < 0.001), with more males (72% versus 47%, respectively, p < 0.001; Table 1 ). Significantly more patients without OSA were never smokers than patients with OSA (57% versus 35%, respectively, p < 0.001), while a positive smoking history was more prevalent in patients with OSA than in those without OSA (35% versus 20%, respectively, p < 0.001). The mean CCI was significantly higher in patients with OSA than in those without OSA (3.4 versus 1, respectively, p < 0.001). In addition, the mean number of COVID‐19 vaccinations prior to COVID‐19 diagnosis was higher in patients with OSA (1.8 versus 1.3, p < 0.001), and more patients had at least one vaccination at least 3 weeks before COVID‐19 diagnosis compared with patients without OSA (84% versus 70%, p < 0.001). There were no significant differences in SES between the patients with and without OSA.

The risk for severe compared with mild COVID‐19 was 4.5 times higher (95% CI: 3.5–5.9) for patients with OSA. The risk for moderate compared with mild COVID‐19 was 4.3 (95% CI: 3.1–5.8) if a person had an OSA diagnosis, while the risk for severe compared with moderate COVID‐19 was not significant between patients with or without OSA. The overall mortality rate was 1.2%, which was significantly higher among patients with OSA compared with patients without OSA (odds ratio [OR] 3.2, 95% CI: 2.3–4.6).

In the OSA group, 287 (29%) patients purchased a CPAP device before their COVID‐19 diagnosis (Table 1 ). Patients who purchased the CPAP device had a higher mean age than patients who did not purchase a CPAP device (62 versus 58 years old, respectively, p < 0.001), a higher proportion of males (78% versus 69%, p = 0.004), a lower percentage of patients who had at least one vaccination at least 3 weeks before COVID‐19 diagnosis (79% versus 85%, p = 0.02), and a lower mean number of COVID‐19 vaccinations prior to COVID‐19 (mean 1.5 versus 1.9, p < 0.001). There were no statistically significant differences in SES, smoking habits and CCI between the groups. A trend toward a higher proportion of patients with severe COVID‐19 was found among patients with OSA who purchased a CPAP device than among patients with OSA without one (10% versus 6%, respectively, p = 0.06). Similar COVID‐19 mortality rates were observed between patients who purchased a CPAP device and those who did not.

In a multivariate analysis of severe versus mild COVID‐19, OSA was associated with an increased risk of severe COVID‐19, which was 1.6 times higher (95% CI: 1.1–2.4) compared with mild disease (Table 2 ). With each increase of 1 year of age, the risk of severe COVID‐19 increased 1.1 times (95% CI: 1–1.1). Female gender was found to be a protective factor with an OR of 0.6 (95% CI: 0.5–0.8). Patients with moderate and high SES had a 1.6 times higher risk of severe COVID‐19 than patients from the low SES group (95% CI: 1.2–2.1 and 95% CI: 1.1–2.3, respectively). For each additional CCI point, the risk for severe COVID‐19 increased by 1.3 times (95% CI: 1.3–1.4). Each additional COVID‐19 vaccine prior to COVID‐19 infection reduced the risk of severe COVID‐19 by half (95% CI: 0.5–0.6). In our partial data regarding smoking habits, no association was found between smoking and risk of severe COVID‐19.

Multivariate analysis of severe versus mild COVID‐19.

Note : () 95% confidence interval.

Abbreviations: CCI, Charlson Comorbidity Index; OR, odds ratio; OSA, obstructive sleep apnea; SES, socioeconomic status.

At least 3 weeks before COVID‐19 diagnosis.

We also performed multivariate analysis of mortality due to COVID‐19 (Table 3 ). Age, as expected, was a significant risk factor, with each increase of 1 year the risk increased by 1.1 (95% CI: 1.1–1.1). Patients at the medium SES had a 1.6 times higher risk to die of COVID‐19 than patients from the low SES (95% CI: 1.1–2.5), while patients from the highest SES had a 3.1 times higher risk than patients from the lowest SES (95% CI: 1.8–5.3). For each additional CCI point, the mortality risk was 1.4 times higher (95% CI: 1.3–1.5). Each additional COVID‐19 vaccine prior to COVID‐19 infection reduced the mortality risk by 70% (OR = 0.3; 95% CI: 0.2–0.3). There was a trend toward lower mortality for females (OR = 0.7; CI: 0.5–1, p = 0.06). There was no increase in mortality risk due to COVID‐19 in our population for patients with an OSA diagnosis or for patients with a positive smoking history. Due to the relatively small number of patients with a CPAP device, we could not analyse its effect in this multivariate analysis.

Multivariate analysis of the mortality due to COVID‐19.

Note : () 95% confidence interval.

Abbreviations: CCI, Charlson Comorbidity Index; COVID‐19, Coronavirus disease 2019; OR, odds ratio; OSA, obstructive sleep apnea; SES, socioeconomic status.

At least 3 weeks before COVID‐19 diagnosis.

In order to understand whether patients with higher SES have a higher risk for severe COVID‐19 and a higher mortality rate due to other known factors such as lower rate of vaccination to COVID‐19 or lower CCI score, we also looked at the correlations between these parameters. Although the correlation between SES and having at least one vaccination was found to be significant, the correlation was low ( r = 0.2). This indicates that slightly more patients in the higher SES had at least one COVID‐19 vaccination. The correlation between CCI and the SES was low ( r ~ 0.055).
sections.discussion:
In this study, we examined if OSA was a risk factor for severe COVID‐19. Patients with OSA were older, had a higher proportion of males, a higher proportion with a smoking history, and a higher mean CCI. These findings are consistent with the literature in which patients with OSA are older, more often males, have a positive smoking history, higher BMI, and comorbidities such as cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, stroke and insulin resistance (Maas et al., 2020 ; Wellman et al., 2022 ; Zeng et al., 2023 ). Patients with OSA had higher vaccination rates, and there was no difference in SES between the groups.

This study demonstrated a 4.5 times higher risk for severe COVID‐19 and a 3.2 times higher mortality risk in patients with OSA than in those without OSA. Multivariate analysis showed that the risk of severe COVID‐19 was 1.6 times higher in patients with OSA than in those without. The higher rate of severe COVID‐19 in patients with OSA was in spite of higher vaccination rates. In a multivariate analysis, it was found that the risk of severe COVID‐19 was 1.1 times higher for each additional year of age, and 1.3 times higher for each additional point of the CCI. In addition, women have a 40% lower risk of developing severe disease. These results are consistent with previous studies that showed that age, male gender and comorbidities are independent risk factors for severe COVID‐19 and death due to it (Attaway et al., 2021 ).

Maas et al. described a similar trend in which in a univariate analysis, patients with an OSA diagnosis had a 5.2 times higher risk for hospitalization and progression to respiratory failure compared with patients without OSA. After adjustment for diabetes, hypertension and BMI, the ORs were 1.65 and 1.98, respectively (Maas et al., 2020 ). In a meta‐analysis, OSA was found to increase the risk of severe COVID‐19 by 1.7 times, ICU admission by 1.76 times, and the need for mechanical ventilation by 1.67 times (Hariyanto & Kurniawan, 2021 ). In other studies, a higher proportion of hospitalization, ICU admission (Kendzerska et al., 2023 ) and mortality (Rögnvaldsson et al., 2022 ) due to COVID‐19 among patients with OSA was also demonstrated. Strausz et al. found that OSA is associated with a 2.93 times higher risk of COVID‐19 hospitalization (Strausz et al., 2021 ). A study among hospitalized patients with COVID‐19, who were evaluated for OSA for the first‐time during hospitalization, found that an increased risk for advanced respiratory support was associated with a higher respiratory event index, oxygen desaturation index, hypoxic burden, and lower minimal SpO 2 (Celejewska‐Wójcik et al., 2023 ).

No increased risk of mortality was found in this study in patients with OSA compared with non‐OSA diagnoses, which is consistent with a study by Kendzerska et al. ( 2023 ). In contrast to this study, an increased risk of mortality has been demonstrated in other studies. Voncken et al. found that the mortality risk is 2.59 times higher in COVID‐19 patients with OSA (Voncken et al., 2022 ). In a meta‐analysis, a 1.74 times higher mortality risk due to COVID‐19 was demonstrated among patients with OSA than among patients without OSA (Hariyanto & Kurniawan, 2021 ). In the multivariate analysis in this study, mortality was increased by 1.1 times for each increase of 1 year of age, and by 1.4 times with each additional CCI point. In addition, there was a trend toward a 30% lower mortality for females. This is consistent with the literature that shows that age, male gender and comorbidities are independent risk factors for mortality due to COVID‐19 (Albitar et al., 2020 ; Dessie & Zewotir, 2021 ; Noor & Islam, 2020 ).

In the multivariate analysis in this study, it was found that each COVID‐19 vaccine decreased the risk of severe disease by half. Similar results have been reported in the literature. Quan et al. showed an OR of 1.55 for the association between OSA and severe COVID‐19‐related hospitalization, adjusted for demographic factors, comorbidities and socioeconomic variables, while boosted vaccination status was a protective factor with an OR of 0.48 (Quan et al., 2023 ). In addition, the analysis showed that each additional vaccine dose decreased mortality risk by 70%. A meta‐analysis by Rahmani et al. showed that the first dose decreased the mortality rate by 68%, while the second dose prevented mortality due to COVID‐19 by 92% (Rahmani et al., 2022 ).

Patients with an OSA diagnosis who purchased CPAP devices were older, more often males, and had lower vaccination rates. A trend toward a higher proportion of severe COVID‐19 was found among patients with OSA who purchased a CPAP device compared with patients with OSA who did not (10% versus 6%, respectively, p = 0.06). Unfortunately, we had no information regarding the severity of OSA. However, it is reasonable to assume that patients who purchased CPAP devices had more severe OSA. In addition, as mentioned above, patients who purchased CPAP devices were older and less likely to be vaccinated against COVID‐19. Due to the relatively small number of patients with CPAP devices (only one died due to COVID‐19), comparisons with patients without the CPAP device were not relevant. Furthermore, purchasing a CPAP device is not necessarily equivalent to CPAP usage, and even patients who use CPAP devices could have stopped using them at the time of COVID‐19 or vice versa. Therefore, conclusions regarding the risk of COVID‐19 for patients using CPAP devices could not be drawn in this study. Sampol et al. showed no association between CPAP treatment and severe COVID‐19 or mortality in hospitalized patients (Sampol et al., 2022 ). On the other hand, Rögnvaldsson et al. found that patients with OSA who were treated with positive airway pressure (PAP) for more than 4 years had an OR of 1.4, whilst those who had been treated for less had an OR of 4.1 for severe COVID‐19, compared with patients with OSA without PAP treatment (Rögnvaldsson et al., 2022 ).

An interesting finding is that patients with moderate and high SES had a 1.6 times higher risk of severe COVID‐19 than patients with low SES. Also, patients from high and medium SES had 3.1 times and 1.6 times, respectively, higher risk to die from COVID‐19 compared with patients from the lowest SES. These results are in spite of a slightly higher COVID‐19 vaccination uptake among patients in the higher SES, even though the CCI was distributed relatively equally over all SES. This result is consistent with our unpublished research on the association between COVID‐19 and the purchase of steroidal inhalers, in which we found that patients with higher SES tended to be less hospitalized due to COVID‐19; however, if hospitalized it was at a more severe disease stage. It is possible that patients from higher SES had medical options other than hospitalization and were more aware of the risk of hospitalization. This could lead to hospitalization under severe conditions. Other studies support a higher mortality among patients with higher SES. Little et al. showed that residence in a high‐poverty area in New York was associated with a 0.61 times decreased risk of mortality compared with residence in a low‐poverty area (Little et al., 2021 ). In a study from the USA, increased mortality due to COVID‐19 was associated with countries with higher per‐capita personal income (Mukherji, 2020 ). However, in a review of the current literature, in most cases hospitalization risk was higher in populations with lower income and greater poverty, and higher mortality was correlated with high levels of unemployment and greater poverty (Wachtler et al., 2020 ).

This study had several limitations. The main limitations were the lack of data regarding the severity of OSA and, as an observational retrospective study, patients were not randomized for CPAP usage or to the COVID‐19 vaccine. In addition, information regarding BMI measured close to COVID‐19 and smoking habits was incomplete. Nevertheless, OSA diagnosis alone was found to be a significant risk factor for severe COVID‐19. One explanation could be that the severity of hypoxia in COVID‐19 (and probably in other respiratory diseases with hypoxia) could be aggravated by apnea–hypopnea in OSA. Further support for the effectiveness of the COVID‐19 vaccine has been demonstrated. However, although patients with OSA were more vaccinated, their COVID‐19 was more severe. As more patients with OSA were vaccinated than patients without OSA (84% versus 70%, respectively), one can only speculate that the severity of COVID‐19 in patients with OSA would have been more severe without vaccinations.

In conclusion, in this study, patients diagnosed with OSA had a higher risk of severe COVID‐19. Further support for the effectiveness of the COVID‐19 vaccine was demonstrated. We recommend close medical follow‐up for patients diagnosed with OSA at times of pulmonary infection, such as COVID‐19. Further studies are needed to associate the severity of OSA disease and CPAP usage, and the severity of disease such as COVID‐19.
